newsitem.title: UK: Kennedy tells IRA call truce or fade off agenda.
newsitem.headline: Kennedy tells IRA call truce or fade off agenda.

text.p: U.S. Senator Edward Kennedy told IRA guerrillas on Saturday to call an immediate truce if they wanted Northern Ireland to keep its place high up on President Bill Clinton's agenda.

"The vast majority of Irish-Americans want the IRA to restore its ceasefire immediately. Violence is not the way forward in Northern Ireland; it never has been in the past quarter century and never will be," he wrote in the Irish Times.

Kennedy, one of the most influential Americans in Irish politics, said that Britain's Labour party, the likely winner of May 1 elections, had promised the IRA's Sinn Fein political wing a seat at peace talks in June in return for an immediate truce.

He was referring to a statement last weekend by Mo Mowlam, Labour's Northern Ireland spokeswoman, who told the Irish Republican Army that a truce now would give the government time to verify its genuineness before the talks resume on June 3.

Sinn Fein is barred from the talks between Protestant, pro-British Unionists and the Catholic-backed Irish nationalist SDLP party since the IRA ended a 17-month truce in February last year and resumed its war against British rule of Northern Ireland.
Kennedy said a new IRA truce "must be for good -- the IRA will have no credibility if it simply turns cease-fires on and off."

If the IRA ended its campaign of attacks on Northern Ireland security forces and British targets now, enough time would have elapsed by June 3 for the truce to have been deemed credible by the next British government and the U.S. administration, he said.

"If a ceasefire has been in place for long enough, the opportunity for progress on Northern Ireland would likely be very high on their (Britain and the U.S.) agenda, and I and many other Irish Americans would certainly encourage it," he said.
"If there is no ceasefire by that time, or only a recent ceasefire, Northern Ireland will understandably be lower on that agenda," he said.

Sinn Fein has played down media speculation of an imminent IRA ceasefire. It says that the guerrillas will not silence their guns until Britain sets a time frame for talks and drops all preconditions such as disarmament.
But Unionists insist that the IRA will have to disarm to prove that the truce is more than a tactical ploy and have threatened to walk out of the talks if Sinn Fein enters.

Kennedy said that Britain's failure to invite Sinn Fein to peace talks during the IRA's 17-month truce because of a row over the disarming of guerrillas had made Sinn Fein sceptical about Britain's desire to negotiate an end to conflict.

"On the other hand Unionists will have legitimate doubts about the sincerity of the next IRA ceasefire, since the first was eventually broken. With than kind of negative thinking on both sides, there is little room for more than one more ceasefire so all of us have to make it count," he said.

Kennedy said British insistence that the IRA show willing to "decommission" its arsenal was wrong. "The handing in of weapons in advance never happened in other peace processes and it won't happen in Northern Ireland," he said.
"Decommissioning is a legitimate issue which the parties must address but it is only one of many issues to be considered and resolved as part of the overall process of agreement."
Clinton threw Washington's wholehearted support behind an Anglo-Irish attempt to build peace talks after the IRA's 1994 ceasefire and has urged that the truce be restored.
